doc.title: Jonathan Scales interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 23, 2025

title: Practice versus living, the middle way
summary: He argues for balance between practice and life experience, drawing on Buddhist philosophy and a bicycle analogy.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yes. I actually had this conversation with someone last night, you know about like practicing. Someone kind of like – I was trying to say the same thing to them. And they were like, “Yeah but how can you get to somewhere if you didn’t practice?” And I’m like yes, you’re right. But also there’s a thin fine line in the balance because you know I think they were talking about how you know practice a lot, or when I was younger how consistent I was. And I would say that like yeah, there were times where like I practiced a lot and there was times when I didn’t practice for weeks. And they were so blown away by that. But I had to explain to them well sure I wasn’t practicing those weeks but I was like living life. I was being a human being. So imagine – the whole point of music is self- expression. If you don’t have stuff to express think about what you can do with the music if you actually have stuff in your life to actually express. So like and I’ll put it to you like this – this is going to be the really weird, vulnerable part of the interview. I can’t believe this is being recorded, I’m saying this. You know I know that like I’m not the greatest most technically proficient steel pan player out there. I know that. Like I’m not the most technically proficient steel pan player in my neighborhood of Brooklyn. You see what I’m saying? But I happen to have worked on my voice as a composer and an artist, and it’s not necessarily about how much time I spent in the practice room. Like if somebody hears my music it’s not because I practiced a lot. It’s because something connected in them and they resonate with my music. You see what I’m saying? Now sure I did have to practice in order to do that, but everything comes in balance. You know the music of mine that people really resonate with is the music of the times I wrote when I was going through some crazy time or like I was channeling something into my music and they are picking up on that. And I would not have had those times if I was just practicing my instrument all day long. So it’s a weird balance. But then you can’t – the better you can express yourself on your instrument the better you can express yourself so you have to practice. So it is like this balance. And I study a lot of Buddhist philosophy and that kind of reminds me of the concept called “the middle way.” You know? The middle way where it’s like it’s not too much of this, not too much of that, and it’s like this ever- adjusting – it’s this ever-adjusting thing that there’s no one right way or wrong way in the

same way where like if you’re riding a bicycle there are certain times when you have to grip the handlebars really hard in order to stay on, and certain times you have to be loose in order to stay on. It depends on the terrain, it depends on the angle of this, all these things, so there’s no one right way that you’re supposed to hold the handles of the bike. You see what I’m saying? There’s no right way of like how many hours am I supposed to practice? You know what I’m saying? Because there’s somebody that can be practicing like a thousand hours a day and you know it might be great. Or it might be someone who just like – a person who is feeling something deeply and then comes up with this melody and then like now everyone is deeply attached to what this person expressed because it resonated with them as a person. You see what I’m saying?
